note: Synthesises technical, legal, ethical and multi stakeholder approaches into one transparency and accountability review.
title: Transparency and accountability in AI systems: safeguarding wellbeing in the age of algorithmic decision-making

reading.body:
This paper synthesizes technical, legal, ethical, and multi-stakeholder approaches to transparency and accountability into a single review.

Synthesizing across those four different approaches is useful because each discipline tends to define transparency differently. A technical definition might mean model interpretability while a legal definition might mean disclosure requirements, and a governance document written from only one perspective will miss what the others require.

As a synthesis of existing work rather than new research, it does not propose a single unified definition of transparency, and does not resolve conflicts between the different disciplinary approaches it reviews.

explain_beginner: As AI systems make increasingly important decisions affecting our lives, we often cannot understand how or why they reached their conclusions. This paper reviews the major obstacles to making AI systems more transparent and accountable, examining technical solutions, legal rules, ethical principles, and how different groups can work together. The research aims to help policymakers create better safeguards so AI benefits people rather than harms them.
explain_business: Organizations deploying AI must navigate legal requirements, ethical expectations, and stakeholder demands for explainability. This review identifies that successful implementation requires coordinated approaches spanning technical design, legal compliance, and stakeholder engagement. Companies that proactively embed transparency and accountability into AI systems reduce regulatory risk, build trust with users and regulators, and create sustainable competitive advantage in an era of increasing AI governance requirements.
explain_practitioner: This synthesis reviews transparency and accountability challenges across four domains: technical implementations, regulatory compliance, ethical frameworks, and multi-stakeholder coordination. The paper consolidates current research on how to make algorithmic decision-making interpretable and answerable to oversight, identifying key strategies for responsible AI governance. Results propose pathways for implementing transparency mechanisms while balancing multiple stakeholder interests in AI system design and deployment.
